definition: Fatuous means smugly foolish; silly and empty of sense.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fatuous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fatuous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The talk show fills its last segment with fatuous predictions delivered in sober confidence — last week a guest guaranteed weather control by June.
A silly remark is lightweight and knows it; a fatuous one is just as empty and expects applause.
Idiotic goes past fatuous — foolishness so complete that even self-satisfaction can't dress it up.

Witless means empty of intelligence — no thought at work anywhere in the remark or the plan — and it passes no judgment on the speaker's mood. Fatuous needs one thing more: the glow of self-congratulation. Witless names the vacancy; fatuous is the vacancy taking a bow.

Asinine is foolishness at full volume — so laughably dumb that the room winces the moment it lands. Fatuous is quieter and vainer: an empty remark that sounds almost reasonable while its speaker beams with pride. Asinine earns its laugh at once; fatuous needs a second look.

Fatuous means smugly foolish; silly and empty of sense.

Milo watched one nature documentary and emerged an expert with a fatuous theory: sharks, he announced at dinner, never bother swimmers who "project calm energy," and he planned to prove it in open water come August.
His sister asked what the sharks were supposed to detect the calm with.
Milo, beaming, said they simply know.
The family let the subject drift out with the tide.
Fatuous is the exact word for Milo's theory because it is smugly foolish — silly, empty of sense, and pleased with itself on top.
Plain foolishness can be humble; the fatuous remark never is.
The self-satisfaction is the fingerprint: this unit's inane describes chatter that's merely empty, but fatuous empties the head and then takes a bow.
Fatuous is the reviewer's scalpel for remarks that are silly, empty, and pleased with themselves — the smugness is what earns the word.
This unit's inane covers content-free chatter with no self-congratulation attached; simplistic, meanwhile, is a charge about oversimplifying something real.
If the fool in question is beaming while he says it, fatuous.

The judges at the student pitch night had heard every kind of bad idea, but the one they still quote came dressed as a good one.
A team in matching blazers unveiled its slogan — 'We disrupt limitation itself' — and smiled as though expecting the trophy on the spot.
Pressed for what the company would actually sell, they explained, with growing satisfaction, that the product was 'the mindset' — nothing more.
One judge later called it the most fatuous pitch of her career: polished, confident, and empty in a way that took the room a full minute to absorb.
The team left convinced they had been too visionary for the judges.
